title: Ladakh to Launch India's First High-Altitude Wildlife Safari on Snow Leopard Trails
excerpt: The newly constituted SHAN Conservation Society has directed forest officials to introduce guided jeep safaris across Hemis National Park and other protected areas, modeled on Kaziranga and Ranthambore.
body:
• Ladakh will introduce India's first high-altitude wildlife safari on popular snow leopard and bird-watching trails, approved by Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena.
  • The safaris will use specially designed open-back vehicles driven by trained local guides, modeled on successful programs at Kaziranga, Ranthambore and other national parks.
  • Ladakh is home to 477 of India's estimated 718 snow leopards, along with more than 38 mammal species and 340 bird species.
  • The initiative aims to curb illegal off-roading and wildlife disturbance while creating sustainable livelihoods for local youth.

Ladakh is set to become the site of India's first high-altitude wildlife safari, with the territory's administration approving guided jeep excursions on snow leopard and bird-watching trails in a move designed to balance booming tourist interest with conservation of one of the world's most fragile ecosystems.

The decision was announced at the inaugural meeting of the Snow Leopard and High-Altitude Nature (SHAN) Conservation Society, chaired by Ladakh Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena, the Times of India reported.

How the Safari Will Work

Saxena directed the forest department to introduce guided jeep safaris modeled on popular national parks such as Kaziranga and Ranthambore, using specially designed open-back vehicles driven by trained local drivers and guides. The safari routes will cover areas including Nubra, Zanskar, Sham, Kargil and Drass — regions known for sizeable populations of the elusive snow leopard and rich avian diversity.

Officials have also been asked to explore safari routes across Hemis National Park, one of the largest national parks in South Asia, as well as the Changthang and Karakoram wildlife sanctuaries. Twenty local youths will be appointed and trained in bird-watching, bird identification and wildlife spotting skills, with all necessary equipment provided by the government.

"These efforts aim at conserving Ladakh's natural heritage so that future generations inherit an ecosystem that is richer, healthier and more resilient. Our vision is to establish Ladakh as a global example of community-led conservation and responsible high-altitude mountain tourism."

— Vinai Kumar Saxena, Lieutenant Governor of Ladakh

Snow Leopard Capital of India

Ladakh's biodiversity makes it a natural candidate for a structured wildlife tourism program. The union territory is home to 477 of India's estimated 718 snow leopards — roughly two-thirds of the national population — according to government data. The region also supports more than 38 mammal species, 340 bird species and 1,800 vascular plant species, drawing a growing stream of wildlife tourists and photographers from around the world.

The snow leopard, classified as "Vulnerable" by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, has become a flagship species for Ladakh's conservation identity. In recent years, specialized expedition operators have built lodges and tracking programs in the Hemis and Uley valleys, with winter sighting success rates improving as conservation efforts expand.

Tackling Illegal Off-Roading

A key motivation behind the safari program is curbing the damage caused by unregulated tourism. Illegal off-roading on fragile alpine terrain has become a growing problem as tourist numbers have surged, disturbing wildlife habitats and damaging vegetation that takes decades to recover at high altitude. By channeling visitors into managed safari routes with trained guides, officials hope to reduce human-wildlife conflict while maintaining tourism revenue.

The SHAN Society, constituted by Saxena on June 16, aims to formulate a comprehensive roadmap for community-led wildlife conservation and waste management, and to promote plastic-free tourism and sustainable livelihood generation across Ladakh.

What's Next

While specific launch dates and pricing have not been announced, the initiative adds to a growing portfolio of eco-tourism attractions in Ladakh. The territory recently announced its inaugural Black-necked Crane Festival, scheduled for August 11–14 across Leh, Tso Kar and Hanle, which will feature guided birdwatching, a crane conservation conference and nighttime stargazing at the Hanle Dark Sky Reserve — India's first designated dark sky sanctuary.

For Indian travelers and the diaspora, the safari represents a new way to experience a region that has rapidly emerged as one of the country's most sought-after destinations, blending adventure with a conservation mission that officials hope will become a global model for high-altitude mountain tourism.
